title: Polvorones
subtitle: Spanish melt-in-the-mouth almond and lard shortbread
excerpt: Polvorones are a Spanish Christmas shortbread made with toasted flour, ground almonds, lard, and cinnamon. You get a very fragile biscuit that crumbles the moment you bite into it. The toasted flour is not optional: it is what gives polvorones their particular nutty, dry flavour.
sourceNotes: Polvorones are a traditional Spanish Christmas confection, associated with Andalusia and particularly the town of Estepa (Seville), where commercial production dates back to the 16th century. The name comes from polvo (dust or powder), referring to the way they crumble when bitten. Traditionally made with lard, though butter versions are common.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Polvorones keep well in an airtight tin for up to 2 weeks. Traditionally they are wrapped individually in squares of tissue or greaseproof paper to keep them intact.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 200 degrees Celsius. Fan oven: 185 degrees Celsius. They bake quickly; check at 10 minutes.

glossaryTerms.definition: A biscuit made with a high proportion of fat to flour, giving a crumbly, sandy texture rather than a chewy one. Polvorones take this to an extreme: they contain no liquid or eggs to bind the dough, only fat. The result is an exceptionally fragile biscuit that crumbles when bitten. Toasting the flour before mixing removes some of its moisture and develops a nutty flavour.

Rendered and clarified pig fat, traditionally used in Spanish polvorones and in British shortcrust pastry. Lard has a higher fat content and different crystal structure from butter, which produces a shorter, more crumbly texture in biscuits. In polvorones, lard is the traditional fat; butter can be substituted for a less authentic but still good result.

items.prepNote: flagged: slug assumed as lard; or use unsalted butter if preferred

content.text: Spread the plain flour in a thin layer on a baking tray. Toast in the oven at 180 degrees Celsius for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring once halfway through, until the flour smells faintly nutty and turns the palest golden colour. Spread the ground almonds on a separate tray and toast for 5 to 7 minutes until lightly coloured. Leave both to cool completely. This step must be done before mixing the dough.

Sift the cooled toasted flour and icing sugar into a bowl. Add the toasted ground almonds and cinnamon. Add the lard (or softened butter) in pieces and the vanilla extract. Mix with your hands until the mixture just comes together into a crumbly dough. It will feel drier and more fragile than a standard biscuit dough; this is correct.
Preheat the oven to 200 degrees Celsius. Line a baking tray with baking paper.

On a clean surface (do not use extra flour), gently press the dough to about 1.5 cm thickness with your hands or a rolling pin. Use a small round cutter (about 4 to 5 cm) to stamp out rounds. Press firmly and lift straight up. Place on the prepared tray. Re-press the scraps very gently once only.

Bake for 10 to 12 minutes. The polvorones are done when the edges are just beginning to colour and the surface looks set but is still very pale. Do not wait for them to look brown; they go from underdone to overdone in under 2 minutes.

Leave on the tray for at least 30 minutes before moving; they are extremely fragile while warm and will break apart if handled too soon. Once cooled, dust generously with icing sugar. Wrap each one individually in a small square of tissue paper or greaseproof paper to protect them.

attrs.problem: The dough will not come together and crumbles apart
attrs.avoid: Avoid adding liquid to bind the dough; polvorones contain no liquid and should not have any added.
attrs.fix: Work the dough a little longer with your hands; the warmth of your palms softens the fat slightly and helps the dough cohese. If it still will not hold together, the lard or butter was too cold; let the dough sit at room temperature for 10 minutes and try again.

attrs.problem: The polvorones break apart when lifted off the tray after baking
attrs.avoid: Avoid moving them while warm; they have almost no structural integrity until fully cooled.
attrs.fix: Leave undisturbed on the tray for at least 30 minutes. Slide a thin palette knife underneath to lift them, supporting the full base rather than levering from one edge.

attrs.problem: The flour tastes raw or starchy in the finished biscuit
attrs.avoid: Avoid skipping or shortening the flour-toasting step; undertreated flour tastes noticeably starchy.
attrs.fix: Toast the flour until it colours slightly and smells nutty; pale cream or very light gold is the target. If in doubt, toast for a further 3 to 4 minutes and test a small pinch for raw starchiness.

content.text: The traditional way to serve polvorones is wrapped individually in coloured tissue paper or squares of greaseproof paper, twisted at both ends. This is not just decorative: the wrapping supports the biscuit and prevents it from crumbling before it reaches the mouth. Eat by holding the wrapped biscuit with both hands, biting, and allowing the crumble to stay contained in the paper.
